Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, May 21, 2026
Toplines
Russia and Belarus completed their combined nuclear exercises on May 21, highlighting Russia’s ability to leverage Belarus for future Russian military operations and Russia’s deepening de facto control over Belarus.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko presided over the second stage of combined Russian-Belarusian nuclear force exercises on May 21.[1] The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that Russian forces delivered nuclear munitions to Belarus and that Belarusian forces practiced receiving, equipping, and moving specialized munitions and launch vehicles for the Iskander-M ballistic missile system.[2] The Russian MoD claimed that the exercises included the launch of a Yars intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) from the Plesetsk State Test Cosmodrome, a Zircon hypersonic missile from the Barents Sea, a Sineva ICBM from a submerged nuclear-powered strategic submarine, cruise missiles from Tu-95MS aircraft, a Kinzhal hypersonic missile from MiG-31I aircraft, and an Iskander-M missile from the Kapustin Yar Training Ground.[3] The Russian MoD claimed that elements of the Russian Strategic Missile Forces, Northern and Pacific Fleets, Long-Range Aviation (Russian Aerospace Forces [VKS]), and Leningrad and Central Military Districts took part in the missile launches.[4] Putin claimed that Russia and Belarus plan to hold the biennial “Union Shield” exercises in 2027. The next Union Shield exercises may include a nuclear component for the first time.
The exercises with Russian nuclear weapons deployed on Belarusian territory highlight the extent to which Russia has absorbed Belarus under its de facto control. The Belarusian Constitution previously stated that Belarus was a non-nuclear state, but Belarus amended its constitution in 2022 to renounce the country’s neutrality and non-nuclear status, likely under Kremlin pressure and influence over Belarusian decision-making.[5] The exercises reflect the deterioration of Belarusian sovereignty and Russia’s expanding capacity to leverage Belarus as a springboard for its own military purposes.
Ukrainian strikes continue to constrain Russian oil refining and energy revenues, even as the war in the Middle East has provided a budget windfall in the short term.
Reuters reported on May 20, citing unspecified official data and sources, that virtually all major oil refineries in central Russia have halted or scaled back their fuel output following recent Ukrainian drone strikes.[6] Reuters reported that the affected refineries total over 30 percent of Russian gasoline output and 25 percent of Russia’s diesel output. The source told Reuters that the Kirishi Oil Refinery in Leningrad Oblast, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries that has a processing capacity of 20 million metric tons per year, has fully halted operations since May 5. Ukrainian forces struck the Kirishi refinery on the night of May 4 to 5.[7] Reuters noted that it is unclear if the Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez Oil Refinery, which has an annual processing capacity of 17 million tons, has been able to maintain partial operations following a Ukrainian strike on May 20.
Reuters also reported on May 20 that Russian oil and gas revenues are set to rise 39 percent year on year in May to 700 billion rubles (about $9.8 billion) due to rising oil prices from the war in the Middle East but that these revenues are expected to decline by 17 percent from April 2026.[8] Reuters noted that Russia’s oil and gas revenues from January to May 2026 declined by about a third year on year to three trillion rubles (about $42.1 billion). Reuters attributed the revenue loss from April to May to increased Russian subsidies for oil refineries and cyclical payments of profit-based tax. Declines in Russian oil revenues from April to May in particular are likely also partially the result of Ukraine’s strike campaign against Russian oil infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have significantly increased the frequency, range, and intensity of such strikes since March 2026, creating outsized impacts on Russian oil exports and refining capacity and undercutting Russia’s ability to profit from increased global oil price spikes.[9] ISW observed reporting in summer-fall 2025 that Russia struggled to repair damage to its oil refineries from Ukrainian strikes, as Western sanctions have restricted Russia’s access to the necessary parts.[10] Russia will likely struggle to repair damages from this most recent intensification in Ukraine’s strike campaign as well. Future Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure will likely continue to strain Russian revenues and prevent Russia from reaping any long-term benefits from the current surge in oil prices.
Russia continues to tap into its gold reserves to cover its budget deficit.
The Russian Central Bank reported on May 20 that Russia’s gold reserves declined for the fourth consecutive month in April 2026.[11] The bank reported that the reserves totaled 73.9 million ounces of gold bars as of May 1, the lowest since March 2022. The report stated that the volume of gold bars decreased by 200,000 ounces in April 2026 and by 900,000 ounces since January 2026. Russian independent newspaper
The Moscow Times
reported, citing the World Gold Council, that Russia lost 27.9 metric tons of gold reserves from January to April 2026, setting a record decline since 2002.[12] The Russian Central Bank resorted to selling its gold reserves for the first time in November 2025 to sustain high wartime spending while Russia has also steadily depleted its sovereign wealth fund’s liquid reserves in order to fund its war in Ukraine.[13] Russia’s growing reliance on its gold reserves underscores its mounting debt pressures as it undertakes difficult decisions to sustain its war in Ukraine.
The Kremlin is attempting to manipulate Russian media coverage to downplay the Kremlin’s censorship campaign, likely to improve the public perception of the United Russia Party ahead of the September 2026 State Duma elections.
Russian opposition source Meduza, citing three employees of pro-Kremlin and state media publications, reported on May 21 that the political bloc of the Russian Presidential Administration has urged state-run and pro-government media sources to avoid using the word “ban” in their articles.[14] The sources stated that the Presidential Administration advised media sources to reduce their coverage of Kremlin bans, restrictions, and fines concerning freedom of speech and expression. One source stated that the media is allowed to cover the Russian government decisions to lift bans, however. One of the sources also noted that the Kremlin expects the media sources to highlight “positive and therapeutic” initiatives from the United Russia Party, including when party members speak out against bans. United Russia General Council Secretary Vladimir Yakushev stated on May 19 that the party is not a “party of prohibitions” and is publicly explaining why the Kremlin should not impose bans and censorship.[15] Russian President Vladimir Putin has recently faced a downturn in public support amidst intensified efforts to restrict access to virtual private networks (VPNs), foreign messaging platforms, and the mobile internet, imposing tangible hardships in the everyday lives of Russians.[16] The Kremlin’s latest restrictions on the media come against the background of brutal efforts to ban the freedom of speech, sending critical milbloggers to frontline assault units in Ukraine or imprisoning them.[17]
Key Takeaways
Russia and Belarus completed their combined nuclear exercises on May 21, highlighting Russia’s ability to leverage Belarus for future Russian military operations and Russia’s deepening de facto control over Belarus.
Ukrainian strikes continue to constrain Russian oil refining and energy revenues, even as the war in the Middle East has provided a budget windfall in the short term.
Russia continues to tap into its gold reserves to cover its budget deficit.
The Kremlin is attempting to manipulate Russian media coverage to downplay the Kremlin’s censorship campaign, likely to improve the public perception of the United Russia Party ahead of the September 2026 State Duma elections.
Ukrainian forces advanced in western Zaporizhia Oblast.
Russian forces launched one ballistic missile and 116 drones toward Ukraine overnight.
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian Operations in the Russian Federation
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian oil refinery in Samara Oblast on May 21.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported on May 21 that Ukrainian forces struck the Syzran Oil Refinery in Samara Oblast, over 800 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.[18] Russian opposition source Astra, citing local residents, reported that a fire started in Syzran after a strike and assessed that eyewitness footage shows smoke rising from the city’s industrial zone.[19] Geolocated footage published on May 21 shows a fire near the refinery.[20] NASA Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) data from May 21 shows heat anomalies in Syzran.[21] Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev acknowledged on May 21 that Ukrainian drones struck industrial targets in Syzran.[22] Rosneft’s Syzran oil refinery has a processing capacity of seven to 8.9 million tons of oil per year and produces gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation kerosene, and bitumen.[23]
Ukrainian forces reportedly struck rail infrastructure in Bryansk Oblast on May 21.
Russian Railways claimed on May 21 that a Ukrainian drone struck a switcher locomotive (a locomotive that maneuvers railway vehicles for short distances) at the Unecha station in Bryansk Oblast.[24] Acting Bryansk Oblast Governor Yegor Kovalchuk claimed that Ukrainian forces struck transport infrastructure in Unecha.[25]
Russia is reportedly building protective structures at an air base in Kaliningrad Oblast.
A Ukrainian source reported that satellite imagery recently collected on May 19 shows that Russian authorities began constructing four aircraft hangers at Kaliningrad’s Chkalovsk Naval Air Base in late April 2026, likely to protect aircraft from reconnaissance and drone strikes.[26]
Russian Supporting Effort: Northern Axis
Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions in the Sumy direction.
A source reporting on the Russian Northern Grouping of Forces claimed that Russian forces reached Ivolzhanske (north of Sumy City) and entered Zapsillya (northeast of Sumy City), indicating that Russian forces are likely infiltrating north of Ivolzhanske and Zapsillya.[27] Geolocated footage published on May 20 shows Ukrainian forces striking Russian forces north of Kindrativka (north of Sumy City) and in eastern Yunakivka (northeast of Sumy City) after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[28]
Russian forces are conducting glide bomb strikes against border settlements in Sumy Oblast, possibly to shape the battlefield ahead of future offensive operations.
Geolocated footage published on May 20 shows Russian FAB-500 glide bomb strikes against Ukrainian forces near Chernatske and Novi Vyrky (both northwest of Sumy City near the international border).[29]
Russian forces are attempting to disrupt Ukrainian vehicle movements in Sumy City.
Geolocated footage published on May 21 shows a Russian fiber optic drone striking Ukrainian vehicles within northern Sumy City.[30]
Russian Main Effort: Eastern Ukraine
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #1
–
Kharkiv Oblast
Russian objective: Push Ukrainian forces back from the international border to create a defensible buffer zone with Belgorod Oblast and approach to within tube artillery range of Kharkiv City
The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) and a Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed that Russian forces advanced northeast of Kharkiv City.
The Russian MoD claimed that elements of the Russian 82nd Motorized Rifle Regiment (69th Motorized Rifle Division, 6th Combined Arms Army [CAA], Leningrad Military District [LMD]) seized Shesterivka (northeast of Kharkiv City).[31] The Russian MoD identified advances to the west (right) bank of the Siverskyi Donets River toward Rubizhne (southwest of Shesterivka) as Russian forces’ next tactical objective.[32] A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed that Russian forces seized Starystya and advanced north of Rybaklyne (both northeast of Kharkiv City).[33] A source reporting on the Russian Northern Grouping of Forces claimed that Ukrainian forces retook lost positions south of Vovchansk.[34]
Russian drone strikes against civilian vehicles are closing major roads in Kharkiv City, forcing Ukrainian forces to use alternative routes and disrupting Ukrainian logistics.
Ukrainian officials reported on May 21 that Russian forces conducted at least four drone strikes against vehicles on the Kharkiv City M-03 ring road since the morning, two of which struck police cars.[35] Ukrainian authorities closed a section of the ring road near the site of the strikes.[36] Bohdan Hladkykh, the director of Kharkiv City’s emergency department, reported that Russian forces conduct drone strikes against police cars as the police officers provide assistance after earlier Russian drone strikes.[37] Kharkiv Oblast Patrol Police Head Viktor Levchenko stated that Russian forces often use sleeper drones against passing vehicles and then strike the police who respond to the scene.[38] Russian forces have been conducting a “human safari” – using tactical drones to “hunt” civilians and civilian infrastructure – in Kherson Oblast and have started to spread the practice to other frontline areas.[39]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Velykyi Burluk direction on May 21.
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #2 – Oskil River
Russian objective: Cross the Oskil River in Kharkiv Oblast and push westward into eastern Kharkiv Oblast and northern Donetsk Oblast
Russian forces continued ground activity toward Kupyansk itself and east and southeast of Kupyansk on the east (left) bank of the Siverskyi Donets River on May 21 but did not advance.
[40]
Russian forces also attacked east and northeast of Borova on May 21 but did not advance.
[41]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Donetsk Oblast
Russian objective: Capture the entirety of Donetsk Oblast, the claimed territory of Russia’s proxies in Donbas, and advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Slovyansk direction on May 21 but did not advance.
[42]
The Russian military command continues to move troops from the Kupyansk direction to reinforce efforts in the Lyman direction.
A source reporting on the Russian Western Grouping of Forces reported on May 21 that the Russian military command plans to move over 1,000 servicemembers to the to the Russian 144th Motorized Rifle Division (20th Combined Arms Army [CAA], MMD) in the Slovyansk direction, mostly from the Russian 272th Tank Division (1st Guards Tank Army [GTA], [Moscow Military District [MMD]) operating near Kurylivka (southeast of Kupyansk).[43] This reported tactical control reassignment is the third observed instance of Russia piecemealing forces for the 144th Motorized Rifle Division in recent days.[44] These reports, if true, would indicate that the Russian military command may have abandoned its efforts to seize Kupyansk at this time.
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Kostyantynivka-Druzhkivka tactical area on May 21 but did not advance.
[45]
Geolocated footage published on May 21 shows Russian forces shelling a Ukrainian position in southern Novodmytrivka (north of Kostyantynivka) in an area where Russian sources previously claimed that Russian forces maintained positions.[46]
The Donetsk Oblast Prosecutor’s Office reported on May 21 that Russian forces struck Druzhkivka with five guided FAB-250 glide bombs, injuring five civilians.[47]
Russian forces continued limited ground attacks in the Dobropillya tactical area on May 21 but did not advance.
[48]
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Pokrovsk direction on May 21 but did not advance.
[49]
Russian forces are deploying additional drone and artillery crews and attempting to innovate tactics in the Pokrovsk direction as they fail to advance.
An officer of a Ukrainian battalion operating in the Pokrovsk direction reported May 21 that Russian forces are deploying additional drone and artillery crews in the Pokrovsk direction and dropping a greater number of KAB guided glide bomb.[50] The officer reported that Russian forces struggle to both conduct assaults and advance. An officer of a Ukrainian brigade operating in the Pokrovsk direction reported May 21 that Russian forces are launching fewer assaults in the units’ area of responsibility compared to this time last year, indicating that Russian forces have taken significant losses.[51]  The officer reported that Russian forces are using electric bicycles to move more stealthily than on motorcycles. The officer reported that Russian forces are increasing their use of unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) but use them five to seven kilometers behind the front line, prioritizing  keeping the UGVs over servicemembers.
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Novopavlivka direction on May 21 but did not advance.
[52]
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Oleksandrivka direction on May 21 but did not advance.
[53]
Russian forces are not advancing in the Oleksandrivka direction despite receiving reinforcements.
The spokesperson of a Ukrainian brigade operating in the Oleksandrivka direction reported on May 21 that Russian forces do not have the initiative and are not advancing or using armored vehicles in the brigade’s area of responsibility.[54] The spokesperson reported that Russian forces attack at most ten times a day, a fivefold decrease from winter 2025-2026. The spokesperson also noted that Russian forces sent reinforcements to units in the Ukrainian brigade’s area of responsibility three times. The spokesperson reported that Russian servicemembers in this area still do not have enough food because of logistical problems, however, and that many Russian servicemembers are convicts or forced conscripts.
Ukrainian forces conducted a long-range strike against a Russian drone pilot training facility in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
The Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) and USF Commander Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi reported on May 20 that Ukrainian forces struck a drone pilot training facility of the Russian Academy of Rocket and Artillery Sciences training servicemembers of the Russian 78th Spetsnaz Sever-Akhmat Regiment (42nd Motorized Rifle Division, 58th Combined Arms Army [CAA], Southern Military District [SMD]) in occupied Snizhne (roughly 135 kilometers from the front line).[55] The USF and Brovdi reported that the strike inflicted 65 casualties, including a lieutenant colonel with call sign “Buryi” who headed the facility, and destroyed production and repair facilities as well as four Tiger armored inside them. Geolocated footage shows an explosion and fire after the strike.[56]
Ukrainian forces conducted medium- and long-range strikes against logistics targets in occupied Donetsk oblast in a continuation of their battlefield air interdiction campaign (BAI) campaign.
Geolocated footage published on May 20 shows Ukrainian forces striking a Russian Ural-4320 truck near occupied Yenakiye (roughly 60 kilometers from the frontline).[57] Geolocated footage published on May 20 shows a burning fuel truck near occupied Manush (roughly 150 kilometers from the front line) along the E-58 Manhush-Osypenko highway, likely after a Ukrainian strike.[58]
Ukrainian forces conducted additional frontline, medium-, and long- range strikes against Russian military assets in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
Brovdi reported May 21 that Ukrainian forces struck  a BM-27 Uragan multiple rocket launcher in Zeleny Hai (on the frontline), a command and observation point of an element of the Russian 6th Tank Regiment (90th Tank Division, 41st CAA, Central Military District [CMD]) in occupied Bahatyr (roughly 20 kilometers from the front line), a command post of the drone unit of the 433rd Motorized Rifle Regiment (27th Motorized Rifle Division, 2nd CAA, CMD) in occupied Selidove (roughly 30 kilometers from the frontline), a drone workshop of the 150th Motorized Rifle Division (8th CAA, SMD) in occupied Donetsk City (roughly 80 kilometers from the frontline), a Russian mobile fire group in occupied Monakhove (roughly 70 kilometers from the frontline), an S-300V air defense system radar and a refueling tanker truck in occupied Shyroka Balka (roughly 160 kilometers from the front line), and additional Russian forces logistics in occupied Donetsk Oblast.[59]
Russian Supporting Effort: Southern Axis
Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City
Russian forces continued infiltration missions northwest to southwest of Hulyaipole on May 20 but did not advance.
[60]
Geolocated footage published on May 20 shows Ukrainian strikes against  Russian forces in northern Varvarivka, central Pryluky, and west of Pryluky(all northwest of Hulyaipole) after what ISW assesses were infiltration missions.[61]
Ukrainian forces continue counterattacking and advancing southeast and northwest of Orikhiv in western Zaporizhia Oblast.
[62]
Geolocated footage published on May 17 indicates that Ukrainian forces recently advanced south of Mala Tokmachka (southeast of Orikhiv), supporting Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets’ May 20 statement that Ukrainian forces liberated Mala Tokmachka.[63]
Ukrainian forces continue their mid-range strike campaign against Russian military and logistics assets in occupied Zaporizhia Oblast.
Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) Commander Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi reported on May 21 reported that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Tor air defense system and a semi-truck in occupied Berestove (about 66 kilometers behind the frontline), a gathering of elements of the 3rd Motorized Rifle Battalion of the Russian 38th Motorized Rifle Brigade (35th Combined Arms Army [CAA], Eastern Military District [EMD]) in occupied Novoukrainka (about 39 kilometers behind the front line), and a port crane in occupied Berdyansk (about 97 kilometers behind the frontline).[64]
Russian forces continued limited ground attacks in the Kherson direction on May 21, but are reportedly struggling to conduct assaults against Ukrainian first-person view (FPV) and fiber optic drone strikes.
[65]
A Ukrainian strike against a portion of the Arabat Spit in occupied Kherson Oblast on the night of May 16 to 17 reportedly struck a Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) command post, killing and wounding about 100 Russian personnel.
[66] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported the Arabat Spit strike and noted that Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system near occupied Shchaslyvtseve (roughly 190 kilometers from the front line).[67] ISW observed reports of Ukrainian forces striking a Russian ammunition depot near the Arabat Spit and a drone and missile storage area in Shchaslyvtseve on the night of May 16 to 17.[68]
Russian Air, Missile, and Drone Campaign
Russian Objective: Target Ukrainian military and civilian infrastructure in the rear and on the front line
Russian forces continued missile and long-range drone strikes against Ukraine overnight on May 20 to 21.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched one Iskander-M ballistic missile from Rostov Oblast and 116 Shahed, Gerbera, and Italmas-type drones and Parodiya decoy drones from the directions of Kursk, Bryansk, and Oryol cities; Millerovo, Rostov Oblast; Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Krasnodar Krai; and occupied Hvardiiske, Crimea.[69] The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Ukrainian forces downed 109 drones, that the Iskander-M and five drones hit five locations, and that drone debris fell on four locations. Dnipropetrovsk Oblast officials reported that Russian forces struck residential areas in Dnipro City, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, injuring at least 14 civilians.[70] Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces also struck Konotop, Sumy Oblast, killing at least one civilian and injuring at least 12.[71] Russian milbloggers claimed that Russian forces struck trains near Kamyanske and Kryvyi Rih, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.[72]
Russia is reportedly expanding its capacity to launch jet-powered Shahed-type drones at Ukraine.
A Ukrainian source focusing on Russian long-range aviation published satellite imagery on May 20 showing that Russia is constructing 10 new drone launch ports compatible with Russian Geran-4 and Geran-5 (Shahed-type) strike drones at the Tsimbulova Airfield in Oryol Oblast.[73] Geran-4 and Geran-5s are newer variants of the Shahed-type long-range strike drones that have jet-powered engines.[74] The Ukrainian source reported that Russian forces are also constructing at least eight new concrete structures to store drones at the airfield. Russia has long been increasing the size of its strike packages against Ukraine and likely intends to use additional drone launch points to increase both the size and diversity of drones used in its nightly strike packages.
Ukraine continues to expand its capacity to counter Shahed-type drones, including jet-powered Shaheds.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov stated on May 21 that Ukrainian forces doubled their interception rate of Russian long-range drones using interceptor drones from January to May 2026 even though Russian forces also increased the number of drones in their strike packages by about 35 percent in the same period.[75] Fedorov stated that Ukraine has also increased the supply of its interceptor drones by 2.6 times from January to May and intends to scale up production by “dozens of times” in order to stockpile interceptor drones to use against jet-powered Shahed drones ahead of fall-winter 2026.
Ukraine is expanding its air defense umbrella to include volunteers from private businesses and regional or local formations.
Fedorov reported that 27 Ukrainian businesses have joined a private air defense project, authorizing Ukrainian companies to perform counter-drone efforts in collaboration with the Ukrainian Air Force.[76] Fedorov reported that two of these businesses are now fully performing air defense operations in Kharkiv and Odesa oblasts. The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD) reported that Ukrainian local governments can finance air defense groups as part of territorial communities, whose operational leadership is in the Ukrainian Air Force and Ukrainian Armed Forces.[77]
Significant Activity in Belarus
Russian efforts to increase its military presence in Belarus and further integrate Belarus into Russian-favorable frameworks
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko stated on May 21 that Belarus has no intention of entering the war in Ukraine.[78]
Lukashenko stated that Belarus would only conduct offensive operations against Ukraine in self-defense. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently warned that Russia was pressuring Belarus to enter the war in Ukraine as a belligerent.[79]

Iran Update Special Report, May 21, 2026
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and
The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute
are publishing daily updates to provide analysis on the war with Iran. The updates focus on US and Israeli strikes on Iran and Iran and the Axis of Resistance’s response to the strikes. The updates cover events from the past 24-hour period.
Key Takeaways
Iran has not submitted a response to the latest US proposal as multiple mediators continue efforts to narrow gaps between the United States and Iran.  Both US and Iranian officials said on May 21 that nuclear weapons and the Strait of Hormuz remain the two “sticking points” on negotiations. Iranian officials appear divided over potential nuclear concessions, especially whether Iran should send its highly enriched uranium (HEU) stockpile abroad. The reporting does not clarify the seniority of the Iranian leakers or clarify their motives, but the contents of the leaks about the alleged directive from Mojtaba and subsequent denials suggest disagreement within the Iranian regime over nuclear concessions.
Iranian officials have coalesced around demands to formalize Iranian control over Strait of Hormuz transit, in contrast to their apparent division over the nuclear file. Iran’s demands over the Strait of Hormuz demonstrate that Iranian officials believe they won the war because formalizing Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz is a territorial claim on the sovereign territory of another country.
Iran continues to attempt to build support for its protection racket in the Persian Gulf, in which vessels must pay, coordinate with, or receive permission from Iran’s preferred mechanism to transit the Strait of Hormuz in order to avoid attacks from Iranian forces.
Iran is continuing to use the ceasefire period to reconstitute its drone and missile program. Iran’s drone program is far more difficult to degrade for long periods of time compared to the ballistic missile program. The drone program relies on less complex and more easily-produced systems compared to the ballistic missile program, which requires huge facilities with extremely specialized equipment (like planetary mixers for solid fuel, for example).
The People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Russia are helping Iran reconstitute its drone and missile program. The PRC has sent missile components, according to US officials familiar with intelligence assessments, speaking to CNN. There is no evidence that these missile components reached Iran.
Toplines
Iran has not submitted a response to the latest US proposal as multiple mediators continue efforts to narrow gaps between the United States and Iran. Both US and Iranian officials said on May 21 that nuclear weapons and the Strait of Hormuz remain the two “sticking points” on negotiations.[1]
Axios reported on May 20 that Pakistan and Qatar drafted a revised memo to bridge US-Iran gaps, while other mediators, including Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Egypt, have supported the effort.[2] Iranian media reported on May 21 that Iran is still reviewing the proposal and has not yet responded.[3] Iranian media added that Iran is discussing the Iranian text’s overarching framework, some details, and confidence-building measures as guarantees.[4] It stated that the text has narrowed some gaps “to some extent,” but that further progress depends on whether the United States moves away from military threats.[5]
Iranian officials appear divided over potential nuclear concessions, especially whether Iran should send its highly enriched uranium (HEU) stockpile abroad.
Two unspecified senior Iranian sources told Reuters on May 21 that Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a directive that Iran’s HEU should remain inside Iran.[6] The sources added that top Iranian officials believe that sending the HEU stockpile abroad would leave Iran more vulnerable to future US and Israeli attacks.[7] An unspecified US official and another unspecified senior Iranian official denied the existence of a directive from Mojtaba on May 21, however.[8] The senior Iranian official confirmed that Iran’s consistent position is to down-blend the stockpile inside Iran, however.[9] Iranian Foreign Affairs Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei stated on May 21 that the negotiations focus on ending the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon, “at this stage,” and that media claims about nuclear issues, including enriched materials or enrichment, “are merely media speculation and lack credibility.”[10]
The reporting does not clarify the seniority of the Iranian leakers or clarify their motives, but the leaks about the alleged directive from Mojtaba and subsequent denials suggest disagreement within the Iranian regime over nuclear concessions.
Top US officials, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have highlighted the “fractures” in the regime in recent days and have noted that these fractures are causing challenges as negotiations continue.[11] ISW-CTP continues to assess that Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi plays a dominant role in policy formation. Vahidi and those around him reportedly previously opposed discussions over the nuclear issue, while the Iranian negotiating team led by Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed the nuclear issue during the first round of US-Iran talks in Islamabad.[12] The Associated Press also noted that Ghalibaf and Araghchi faced “criticism” for showing too much willingness to make concessions in Islamabad.[13] Ghalibaf and Araghchi reportedly discussed the nuclear issue “contrary to instructions from Tehran.”[14] Such instructions, ISW-CTP noted at the time, could have only come from Vahidi or the supreme leader.[15] The leaks and denials about Mojtaba’s directive on May 21 are emblematic of this debate, which has been playing out since April.
Iranian officials have coalesced around demands to formalize Iranian control over Strait of Hormuz transit, in contrast to their apparent division over the nuclear file. Iran’s demands over the Strait of Hormuz demonstrate that Iranian officials believe they won the war because formalizing Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz is a territorial claim on the sovereign territory of another country.
Iran released a map of a Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA)-defined maritime zone on May 20.[16] The PGSA’s new map appears to expand Iran’s claimed management zone beyond the area Iran previously depicted on May 4.[17] The new PGSA-defined zone runs from Kuh Mobarak in Iran to southern Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in the east and from the end of Gheshm Island in Iran to Umm al Qaiwain in the UAE in the west.[18] This change lays explicit claim to control over the territorial waters of the UAE and Oman.
Iran continues to attempt to build support for its protection racket in the Persian Gulf, in which vessels must pay, coordinate with, or receive permission from Iran’s preferred mechanism to transit the Strait of Hormuz in order to avoid attacks from Iranian forces.
Iranian Ambassador to France Mohammad Amin Nejad told Bloomberg on May 21 that Iran and Oman are discussing a permanent toll system to formalize control over maritime traffic through the strait.[19] Iranian officials and state media also reported that commercial vessels coordinated with IRGC Navy forces to transit the strait, while IRGC framed this coordination as necessary for safe passage.[20] US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated on May 21 that an Iranian toll system would be unacceptable and “would make a diplomatic deal unfeasible,” which shows that Iran’s Strait demands remain a major obstacle to any US-Iran agreement.[21] ISW-CTP previously assessed that allowing Iran to continue enforcing protocols would be detrimental to US and international commercial interests, as it would mean Iran could prevent ships from traversing the strait anytime it wants.[22]
Iran is continuing to use the ceasefire period to reconstitute its drone and missile program.
Sources familiar with US intelligence assessments on Iranian reconstitution told CNN on May 21 that Iran will likely be able to reconstitute damage to Iran’s defense industrial base “in a matter of months, not years,” which is “much faster” than the US intelligence community estimated.[23] This information does not clarify which elements of the defense industrial base or how specific reconstitution would result in changes to reconstitution timelines, which makes the information difficult to judge on its own merits. These timelines are impossible to evaluate without answering such questions, and the assumptions underlying these timelines should be rigorously interrogated, therefore. The officials partially attribute this to some of Iran’s defense industrial base remaining intact.[24] Iran has reportedly been replacing missile sites, launchers, and production sites destroyed during the airstrikes.[25] It is unclear what constitutes a “production site” in this context. A production site could theoretically range from an entire factory complex (which would need to be rebuilt if destroyed) to a single piece of complex but rapidly replaceable machinery. The lack of clarification also makes this evaluation difficult to judge on its own merits. Iran still has 50 percent of its drone capabilities, which amounts to thousands of drones, as well as a “large percentage” of Iran’s coastal defense cruise missile stockpile left, according to these officials.[26] Iran’s drone program is far more difficult to degrade for long periods of time compared to the ballistic missile program. The drone program relies on less complex and more easily-produced systems compared to the ballistic missile program, which requires huge facilities with extremely specialized equipment (like planetary mixers for solid fuel, for example). The officials observed that Iran has around two-thirds of its missile launchers after digging out many during the ceasefire.[27] CNN noted that this estimation may still include buried launchers, however.[28]
The People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Russia are helping Iran reconstitute its drone and missile program.
The PRC has sent missile components, according to US officials familiar with intelligence assessments, speaking to CNN.[29] There is no evidence that these missile components reached Iran. CNN added that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports may have hindered Russian and Chinese efforts to support Iran’s reconstitution.[30] US Central Command (CENTCOM) reported that US forces redirected 94 vessels and disabled four others since the start of the blockade on Iranian ports on April 13.[31] US forces previously seized the Iranian-flagged
Touska
in the Gulf of Oman on April 19, and its cargo, which was described as “conditional contraband,” including electronic components, computer systems, machinery, and power generation equipment.[32] Unspecified security sources told Reuters that the
Touska
was likely transporting dual-use items from the PRC to Iran because the vessel had done so previously.[33] The PRC has sent multiple shipments of missile fuel precursors to support Iranian missile reconstitution efforts following the June 2025 Israel-Iran War, even during the most recent war.[34] US officials told the
New York Times
on May 9 that Russia is shipping drone components to Iran through the Caspian Sea to help rebuild Iranian drone capabilities as well.[35]
Maritime Developments
See topline section.
US and Israeli Air Campaign
Nothing significant to report.
Iranian Internal Dynamics
See topline section.
Lebanese Hezbollah and the Israeli Campaign in Lebanon
The US Treasury Department sanctioned on May 21 four Hezbollah political officials, two Amal Movement members, two Lebanese officials, and Iran’s ambassador-designate to Lebanon for impeding Hezbollah’s disarmament.
[36] The Treasury Department sanctioned the head of Hezbollah’s Executive Council, who is responsible for reorganizing Hezbollah’s administrative and institutional structure in order for the group to remain armed in Lebanon.[37] The Treasury Department also sanctioned two Hezbollah parliamentarians involved with Hezbollah’s media outreach and a third Hezbollah parliamentarian whom Treasury described as a “key figure” opposing Hezbollah’s disarmament.[38] The Treasury Department sanctioned two Amal Movement security officials.[39] The Amal Movement is a longtime Hezbollah political ally, but ISW-CTP has previously noted that Amal Movement head Nabih Berri has distanced the party from Hezbollah due to disapproval of Hezbollah’s attacks on Israel.[40] The Treasury Department noted that one of the Amal Movement officials, the Amal Security Director, had coordinated public “displays of force” with Hezbollah leadership in order to intimidate Hezbollah’s political opponents in Lebanon.[41] The other sanctioned Amal Movement security official commands the party’s militia in southern Lebanon, which has conducted combined attacks with Hezbollah targeting Israel.[42] The Treasury Department sanctioned the Lebanese Armed Forces’ Intelligence Directorate Bureau Chief responsible for Hezbollah’s Dahiyeh stronghold and the head of the General Directorate for General Security’s National Security Department for sharing intelligence with Hezbollah in the past year.[43] The General Directorate for General Security is Lebanon’s primary intelligence organization.[44] The Treasury Department also sanctioned the Iranian ambassador-designate to Lebanon, whom the Lebanese government declared persona non grata in March and ordered to leave Beirut.[45]
Other Axis of Resistance Activity
Nothing significant to report.

Russian Occupation Update, May 21, 2026
Key Takeaways
Russian officials are preparing to transfer a child from the Oleshky Boarding School to Russia for a medical operation, potentially in violation of international humanitarian law.
Russia continues to facilitate the temporary deportation of teenagers to Russia for military-style training or psychological rehabilitation.
The Russian Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives (PFKI) is spending billions of rubles on the “cultural integration” of occupied Ukraine.
Russian video game developers have designed a game meant to emulate and valorize the first few months of the Russian occupation of Mariupol.
Luhansk Oblast occupation officials introduced a system to automatically assign newborns SNILS (individual insurance account registration numbers), integrating them into Russia’s coercive bureaucracy from birth.
Russian majority state-owned VTB Bank continues to spread its influence in occupied Ukraine via savings accounts.
Russian occupation officials and development companies continue efforts to incentivize Russian investment and facilitate potential resettlement in occupied Ukraine.
The Russian government is moving towards formalizing lower barriers of entry to purchasing real estate in occupied Ukraine via the federal Territorial Development Fund.
Russia is implementing plans to restart production at the Ilyich Steel and Iron Works Plant in occupied Mariupol.
Deportation and Forcible Transfer of Ukrainian Citizens, Including Children
Russian officials are preparing to transfer a child from the Oleshky Boarding School to Russia for a medical operation, potentially in violation of international humanitarian law. Russia has already transferred or deported over eighty residents from the boarding school, which specifically treats children and adults with complex neurological or physical disorders.[1]
Russian newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda’s occupied Kherson Oblast branch reported on May 13 that the Russian Ministry of Health dispatched Russian medical professionals, including pediatric surgeons, to occupied Skadovsk to examine children from the Oleshky Boarding School, which Russian officials previously evacuated to Skadovsk in late 2022.[2] Komsomolskaya Pravda Kherson reported that the medical specialists decided that one child from the Oleshky Boarding School requires a specialized operation and are arranging for their transport to Rostov-on-Don for surgery. Russia took over the Oleshky Boarding School in 2022 and has forcibly removed or deported at least 84 disabled children and adults from the facility in the years since.[3] Many of the children and adults have legal guardians in Ukrainian-held areas, further disproving Russia’s “guardianship” claims to these individuals.[4] Kremlin-appointed Commissioner for Children’s Rights Maria Lvova-Belova and her sister have notably both been personally implicated in the deportation of special needs adults from the Oleshky Boarding School to Penza Oblast.[5]
Russia’s treatment of disabled children and adults, particularly from the Oleshky Boarding School, contravenes its international legal responsibilities. Should a child require specialized medical care, Russia first and foremost should facilitate the transportation of that child to either Ukraine or a neutral third-party state — not unilaterally decide to deport the child to Russia for treatment.[6] In case of absolute medical necessity wherein Russia is the only safe option for the treatment of the child, Russia must ensure the transfer is temporary and provide the Central Tracing Agency of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) with full identification of the child and where in Russia it will be treated.[7] It is unclear, and unlikely, that Russia has met these international legal requirements in preparing for the treatment of the child from the Oleshky Boarding School. Russia has routinely used the guise of medical treatment to deport Ukrainian children to Russia, some of whom are adopted into Russian families and effectively disappeared into the Russian administrative system.[8]
Russia’s “Time of Young Heroes” program is facilitating the temporary deportation of Ukrainian teenagers to Russia for the explicit purpose of military training.
Director of the occupied Zaporizhia Oblast branch of the Voin military-patriotic training camp program Alexey Lukin reported on May 17 that Voin is organizing trips for teenagers aged 14 to 17 from occupied Zaporizhia Oblast to attend military sports sessions as part of Time of Young Heroes at the Avangard sports camp in Volgograd Oblast.[9] Lukin noted that teenagers will learn tactical medicine and drone operation and will interact with Russian veterans and active servicemembers of the war in Ukraine. Avangard will host multiple Time of Young Heroes sessions over the course of Summer 2026. ISW reported on Time of Young Heroes in Summer 2025 and assessed that the program was meant to ideologically indoctrinate Ukrainian youth by exposing them to Russian military-patriotic ideals while also materially preparing them for future service in the Russian military.[10] The Yale Humanitarian Research Lab notably identified the Avangard camp in Volgograd Oblast as a location where Russian officials have taken Ukrainian children for participation in militarization and re-education programs.[11]
The Mariupol occupation administration continues to send vulnerable and traumatized teenagers to Vladimir Oblast for “psycho-emotional” rehabilitation.
Mariupol occupation head Anton Koltsov reported on May 15 that the Vladimir Oblast and Donetsk Oblast occupation governments sent 47 teenagers from occupied Mariupol to the Sheredar health and rehabilitation center in Sosnovyi Bor, Vladimir Oblast.[12] Koltsov noted that these teenagers are “facing difficult life situations” and have been affected by “the fighting,” apparently suggesting that these teenagers are experiencing particular traumas as a result of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The Mariupol occupation administration previously sent a group of families from Mariupol to Sheredar in March 2026 for “psychological and social rehabilitation.”[13] Russia has routinely weaponized psychiatric treatment as a pretext to transfer Ukrainians, particularly children and youth, to Russia and expose them to re-education and indoctrination programs.[14]
Sociocultural Control
The Russian Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives (PFKI) is spending billions of rubles on the “cultural integration” of occupied Ukraine.
PFKI, which Russian President Vladimir Putin personally established by decree in May 2021, held a press conference with Kremlin newswire TASS on May 18 in honor of its five-year anniversary.[15] Deputy Head of the Presidential Directorate for Public Projects Alexander Zhuravsky and PFKI CEO Roman Karmanov both stressed the role that PFKI is playing in the integration of occupied Ukraine into the Russian cultural sphere.[16] Zhuravsky noted that since 2022, PFKI has funded approximately 1,000 projects in occupied Ukraine, totaling 8.5 billion rubles ($120 million). Zhuravsky stated that PFKI “allocates significant resources and supports important projects to support artistic understanding of the special military operation (invasion of Ukraine) across a wide range of artistic forms.” Karmanov noted that over one-third of PFKI’s projects in occupied Ukraine are museum-related, including many that present the Kremlin-approved pseudo-historical justification for the invasion of Ukraine.[17] PFKI’s funding for “cultural integration” in occupied Ukraine underscores the Kremlin’s direct involvement in the state-directed destruction of Ukrainian sociocultural identity in occupied areas.
Militarization of Occupied Areas
Russian video game developers have designed a game that emulates and valorizes the first few months of the Russian occupation of Mariupol.
Occupied Donetsk Oblast-based outlet Donetsk News Agency (DAN) reported on May 18 that youth from occupied Donetsk Oblast, Russian veterans who participated in the seizure of Mariupol, and war correspondents attended a launch event for the Kuindzhi 93 first-person view video game.[18] Kuindzhi 93 allows players to experience Russia’s seizure and occupation of Mariupol through the eyes of a fictional 18-year-old volunteer. The launch event included several “themed interactive zones” where teenaged participants could “walk through a location that recreated the workings of a filtration center.”  Kuindzhi 93 has the clear intent of socializing and normalizing with Ukrainian youth the intense violence that Russian inflicted on Mariupol during the siege and occupation of the city. The apparent gamification and normalization of the filtration process is particularly noteworthy — various open-source and government investigations, including by the United States Department of State, found that Russia’s filtration of Ukrainians at the same sort of filtration centers that Kuindzhi 93 seeks to recreate were intended to suppress Ukrainian resistance and constituted threats to the health and human rights of Ukrainian civilians.[19]
Administrative and Bureaucratic Control
Luhansk Oblast occupation officials introduced a system to automatically assign newborns SNILS (individual insurance account registration numbers), integrating them into Russia’s coercive bureaucracy from birth
. Russian newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda’s occupied Luhansk Oblast branch claimed on May 15 that Luhansk Oblast occupation officials introduced an automatic system to assign SNILS to newborns.[20]
Immediately after a newborn’s registration at the Civil Registry Office, the system transfers their data directly to the Russian Social Fund, assigns them an SNILS, and notifies their mother’s personal account on the Russian Unified Public Services (Gosuslugi) portal.[21] If the mother does not have a verified account, she can obtain the document at the Social Fund’s client service or at a Multifunctional Center upon presentation of her Russian passport and the child’s birth certificate.[22] This automatic system has issued over 12,000 SNILS in occupied Luhansk Oblast since 2024.[23] The automatic assignment of SNILS forces all newborns born in occupied Luhansk Oblast to hold Russian documentation, effectively presenting them as Russian citizens from birth. Russia uses a wide variety of bureaucratic tools to manufacture the impression that occupied Ukraine is populated mainly by Russian citizens.[24]
Occupation Administration Mismanagement and Internal Dynamics
Nothing significant to report.
Physical and Legal Repressions
Nothing significant to report.
Economic and Financial Control
Russian majority state-owned VTB Bank continues to spread its influence in occupied Ukraine via savings accounts.
Occupied Ukraine-based outlets reported on May 14 that VTB’s portfolio of liabilities (the total sum of VTB’s borrowed and acquired funds and equity) in occupied Ukraine has increased by 13 percent since the beginning of 2026, amounting to almost 23 billion rubles ($323 million).[25] VTB’s director for occupied Ukraine Viktor Shiip claimed that VTB has observed a “rapid increase” in the use of VTB savings accounts in occupied areas. VTB recently reported that the volume of investments in VTB savings products in occupied Ukraine grew by 10 percent in the first three months of 2026.[26] VTB’s expanded influence in the financial sphere in occupied Ukraine means that it has greater control over the financial outcomes of residents of occupied areas. Russian state-owned banks writ large have become a critical tool of Russia’s occupation of Ukraine and may even be complicit in war crimes due to their integration with the overall occupation apparatus.[27]
Information Space Control
Nothing significant to report.
Infrastructure and Development Projects
Russian occupation officials and development companies continue efforts to incentivize Russian investment and facilitate potential resettlement in occupied Ukraine.
The Russian Evolutsiya development company claimed on May 15 that low barriers to real estate market entry and two percent preferential mortgages are attracting buyers to occupied Donetsk Oblast from all over Russia.[28] Evolutsiya claimed that buyers from large Russian cities including Kazan, Yekaterinburg, Chelyabinsk, St. Petersburg, and Moscow are investing in real estate in occupied Donetsk Oblast, and noted that the housing and development market in occupied Mariupol is particularly lucrative for Russian investors. Evolutsiya’s reporting on Russian buyers in the real estate market in occupied Ukraine echoes recent statements made by other Russian officials suggesting that Russians account for the majority of housing purchases in occupied areas, including 75 percent of apartment purchases in occupied Mariupol.[29]  Kherson Oblast occupation head Vladimir Saldo claimed on May 14 that his administration continues to implement the two percent preferential mortgage rate and also offers up to 12 percent preferential mortgages on housing for Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine.[30] Russia has used such financial incentives to draw Russian investment to occupied Ukraine, which in many cases supplements the broader campaign to incentivize Russian resettlement in occupied areas.[31] Russian officials have claimed that such incentives are already having a bearing on the population of occupied areas — Mariupol occupation deputy head Ignat Yeremchuk claimed on May 17 that the population of occupied Mariupol has risen to nearly 330,000 from around 100,000 in early 2022 due to job availability, infrastructure projects, and construction.[32] Pro-Russian users on Telegram have criticized Yeremchuk’s claimed number, however, noting that Mariupol’s population is around 200,000 maximum.[33] The Russian government has the incentive to inflate population numbers for informational effects aimed both at encouraging domestic audiences to move to occupied Ukraine and aimed at international audiences to create the impression that these occupied areas are intrinsically Russian.
The Russian government is moving towards formalizing lower barriers of entry to purchasing real estate in occupied Ukraine via the federal Territorial Development Fund
. The Russian State Duma adopted a draft law in its first reading that would allow tenants of properties owned by the Russian Territorial Development Fund in occupied Ukraine to purchase the properties without going through a bidding process.[34] The Territorial Development Fund is a subordinate entity to Russia’s Ministry of Construction and is a key instrument for Russia’s administrative and economic integration of occupied areas, managing investment activity, land leases, and infrastructure development.[35] The Territorial Development Fund has previously been involved in activities intended to encourage Russians to relocate to occupied Ukraine.[36] The new draft law, if finalized, will allow the Territorial Development Fund even greater oversight into the allocation of property in occupied Ukraine, which will likely increase the fund and associated individuals’ prospects for self-enrichment by removing the bidding and legal tender processes.
Russia is implementing plans to restart production at the Ilyich Steel and Iron Works Plant in occupied Mariupol.
Mariupol deputy occupation head Ignat Yaremchuk claimed on May 16 that the Russian federal government and the Ministry of Industry and Trade have outlined plans for the Ilyich Plant, which an unnamed investor has begun implementing.[37] Yaremchuk did not give a timeline for the restoration of full production at the Ilyich Plant, which was the second largest metallurgical plant in Ukraine prior to the full-scale invasion. Russia’s invasion caused significant damage to the plant in 2022, and Russian and occupation officials have been trying to pour money into the plant since 2023 in order to restart operations. Russia’s interest and investment in the Ilyich Plant is reflective of its wider extractive economic policy in Ukraine, as the plant has significant economic and defense industrial potential for Russia.[38]
